SINGAPORE – Commuters can expect more reliable and smoother trips on the Bukit Panjang LRT (BPLRT) after extensive system and hardware upgrades are completed by the end of 2026.

The upgrades include replacing 16.6km of power rails that supply electricity to the trains, which is now close to completion, with about 98% of the work done. The renewal works, which started in 2018, also include the replacement of the BPLRT signalling system with a new communications-based train control signalling system like the ones used on MRT lines.

The signalling system enables trains to exchange real-time location and speed data with trackside systems. Trackside systems monitor the location of trains within their zone, calculate safe distances between them, and signal trains to speed up or slow down.

Operations control centre systems – which oversee real-time train operations, network safety and efficiency – were also upgraded. Operations control centre systems – which oversee real-time train operations, network safety and efficiency – have been upgraded.

The Land Transport Authority (LTA), in a statement on Oct 15, said the upgrades have helped boost BPLRT reliability indicators. For instance, trains on the LRT system clocked 443,000 car-km between delays in September 2026, up from 53,000 car-km in 2017.

articles.headline: Singaporean Physicist Aims to Dispel Nuclear Energy Myths
articles.dek: Ian Ang, a nuclear scientist at NUS, is working to counter public misconceptions about nuclear energy, citing safety records and waste management solutions.
articles.lead: Ian Ang, a nuclear energy scientist at the NUS Singapore Nuclear Research and Safety Institute (SNRSI), is actively working to address public skepticism surrounding nuclear power. He encounters frequent opposition, often stemming from historical accidents like Chernobyl and Fukushima.
articles.takeaway: Ian Ang, a nuclear scientist at NUS, is working to counter public misconceptions about nuclear energy, citing safety records and waste management solutions.
body: Ian Ang, a nuclear energy scientist at the NUS Singapore Nuclear Research and Safety Institute (SNRSI), is actively working to address public skepticism surrounding nuclear power. He encounters frequent opposition, often stemming from historical accidents like Chernobyl and Fukushima.

Ang points out that while the Chernobyl disaster resulted in deaths among emergency responders and some thyroid cancer cases, the UN concluded in 2020 that there were no direct radiation-related deaths from the Fukushima incident. He attributes the Chernobyl accident primarily to human error and design flaws rather than the technology itself.

His interest in nuclear energy was sparked over a decade ago when he learned about the Singapore Government's $63 million investment in nuclear safety research. Ang believes nuclear energy offers a strong safety record, low greenhouse gas emissions, and a potential solution to Singapore's resource constraints.

Currently, Ang is researching methods for underground geological repositories to store nuclear waste, noting that the global volume of spent nuclear fuel since the 1950s is equivalent to just 10 Olympic-sized swimming pools, a manageable amount compared to existing storage capacities.

While Singapore has not committed to nuclear energy, Ang is dedicated to advancing the scientific understanding necessary for its potential future implementation, emphasizing the industry's comprehensive lifecycle management.

articles.headline: Singapore Explores Small Modular Reactors for Future Energy Needs
articles.dek: The nation is reassessing nuclear power, focusing on advanced technologies like SMRs, to enhance energy security and meet climate goals amidst global instability.
articles.lead: Singapore is actively examining the potential of nuclear energy, particularly small modular reactors (SMRs), as a component of its future energy mix. This shift in consideration comes after a 2022 report suggested nuclear power could supply up to 10% of the country's electricity by 2050. The move acknowledges the limitations of Singapore's options for emissions reduction in a land-constrained environment and a fragmented geopolitical landscape.
articles.takeaway: The nation is reassessing nuclear power, focusing on advanced technologies like SMRs, to enhance energy security and meet climate goals amidst global instability.
body: Singapore is actively examining the potential of nuclear energy, particularly small modular reactors (SMRs), as a component of its future energy mix. This shift in consideration comes after a 2022 report suggested nuclear power could supply up to 10% of the country's electricity by 2050. The move acknowledges the limitations of Singapore's options for emissions reduction in a land-constrained environment and a fragmented geopolitical landscape.

Advanced nuclear technologies like SMRs are being highlighted for their compact size, factory-assembly potential, and ability to be sited closer to urban centers. This contrasts with Singapore's 2012 decision to rule out conventional nuclear plants due to safety concerns for the densely populated city-state, though it had then left the door open for future technologies.

The renewed interest is driven by a combination of factors, including geopolitical instability impacting global energy supplies, the urgent need for decarbonization, and significant advancements in nuclear technology. Singapore currently relies on natural gas for approximately 95% of its energy needs, but recent global energy crises have underscored the vulnerability of such dependencies.

To bolster its capacity for studying nuclear energy, Singapore plans to undergo a readiness assessment by the UN atomic watchdog in 2027 and has signed multiple agreements with international entities in the nuclear sector. The government has not yet made a final decision on adopting nuclear power, but is actively building its understanding of the technology and its implications for energy security and climate commitments.

This initiative seeks to elevate standards in patient safety, clinical governance, service quality, and professional competence within the TCM sector. Five TCM providers have already been granted the first Accredited TCM Clinic status for meeting these new benchmarks.
articles.takeaway: A new voluntary program aims to enhance standards and public trust in the TCM sector, with five initial clinics receiving accredited status.
body: Singapore has introduced a new voluntary Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) Accreditation Programme, with applications opening on October 17. This initiative seeks to elevate standards in patient safety, clinical governance, service quality, and professional competence within the TCM sector. Five TCM providers have already been granted the first Accredited TCM Clinic status for meeting these new benchmarks.

The program includes accreditation for both TCM service providers and individual practitioners. Service providers will be evaluated on aspects like governance, hygiene, and medication management, while practitioners will be assessed on their qualifications, experience, and professional standing. The Academy of Chinese Medicine, Singapore, has been appointed as the accrediting body.

Health Minister Ong Ye Kung stated that the accreditation goes beyond basic licensing, signifying a commitment to robust governance and public confidence. He highlighted that accredited providers may have opportunities to collaborate with the Ministry of Health on future TCM care models and national healthcare initiatives.

Further initiatives are underway to integrate TCM into the broader healthcare system. The Ministry of Health is exploring allowing accredited TCM practitioners to order X-rays in collaborative care arrangements with general practitioners. Additionally, the TCM Integrative Sandbox initiative will test selected TCM treatments in public hospital settings to assess their safety, effectiveness, and cost-efficiency.

The Ministry of Health is also developing a proof-of-concept initiative to explore collaboration between TCM practitioners and General Practitioners within Singapore's national preventive health strategy, Healthier SG. This initiative aims to leverage the natural overlap between TCM's focus on diet, exercise, and lifestyle modifications and modern preventive medicine.

articles.headline: Singapore Offers Grants for Electric Harbour Craft Transition
articles.dek: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore is providing financial incentives to encourage the adoption of electric vessels, aiming for net-zero emissions by 2050.
articles.lead: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) is launching a grant scheme to support harbour craft operators in switching to electric vessels. The initiative aims to offset costs and promote the early adoption of greener maritime technology.
articles.takeaway: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore is providing financial incentives to encourage the adoption of electric vessels, aiming for net-zero emissions by 2050.
body: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) is launching a grant scheme to support harbour craft operators in switching to electric vessels. The initiative aims to offset costs and promote the early adoption of greener maritime technology.

Under the scheme, operators can receive grants of up to $250,000. The funding is tiered based on a vessel's battery capacity, with $250 disbursed for every kilowatt-hour. The maximum grant amount is capped based on vessel size, with smaller craft eligible for up to $150,000 and larger vessels for the full $250,000.

The grant program will run for two years, officially commencing on January 1, 2027. However, any fully electric vessel that obtains a harbour craft license between October 14, 2026, and December 31, 2028, will qualify for the incentive.

This initiative is part of Singapore's broader strategy to achieve net-zero emissions for the harbour craft sector by 2050. The sector, which currently comprises over 1,600 diesel-powered vessels, faces a significant transition, as vessels typically have a service life exceeding 20 years. By 2030, all new harbour craft operating in Singapore's waters must be fully electric, capable of using B100 biofuel, or compatible with net-zero fuels.

articles.dek: Dealers and analysts say some mass-market vehicles could lose resale value under the proposed COE changes, while demand for pre-owned luxury cars may rise. Pre-owned cars for sale at CarTimes Automobile.

(Image: CNA) SINGAPORE: Proposed changes to the Certificate of Entitlement (COE) system could reshape the used car market, with industry players saying that some mass market vehicles may lose resale value while pre-owned luxury cars could become more attractive to buyers.

The Land Transport Authority (LTA) has proposed merging categories A and B, which classify cars by engine size and power, into a single COE category, and introducing fees and rebates for different car models based on their open market value (OMV).

Under the proposed fee-and-rebate system, the maximum price difference between a higher-end car and a mass-market car would be S$30,000 (US$23,000). Car dealers told CNA that this could change the price gap between new and second-hand vehicles.

For mass-market models that stand to benefit from such rebates, lower prices for new vehicles could put pressure on the resale value of comparable used cars. "Consumers are all competing within the same market," Mr Benjamin Loo, chief operating officer of CarTimes Automobile, said.

"If a consumer is able to buy a brand-new vehicle for S$15,000 less, they might reconsider buying a one-year-old pre-owned vehicle. Dealers will have to remain competitive because it does not make sense for a used vehicle to be priced the same as, or higher than, a brand-new one." Existing owners of newer mass-market cars could also face lower trade-in values if cheaper new vehicles put downward pressure on used-car prices, Mr Loo said.

body: Two men, identified as Chinese nationals Shu Zaijun, 54, and Dong Bangjun, 59, have been charged with theft in relation to incidents that occurred on a Vietjet flight from Ho Chi Minh City to Singapore on October 12.

Shu is accused of stealing two debit cards from a passenger's bag around 8:30 AM, while Dong allegedly stole a credit card from another passenger's bag approximately 30 minutes later. The court documents do not specify if the two men were collaborating on these alleged thefts.

Both men were arrested at Changi Airport Terminal 4 on October 12 after three bank cards belonging to other individuals were found in their possession. The police conducted an operation at the terminal following the discovery.
If convicted, each man faces a jail sentence of up to three years, a fine, or both. Shu's case has been adjourned to October 16, and Dong's case will be mentioned again on October 28.

In-flight theft cases, sometimes linked to syndicates, have seen an increase, with the police noting a rise in the number of people charged in recent years. The Airport Police Division commander previously stated that timely reporting is crucial for officers to track and apprehend suspects before they depart.

SINGAPORE – Two men are set to be charged on Oct 14 after they allegedly stole bank cards from passengers’ bags on a flight from Vietnam’s Ho Chi Minh City to Singapore.

In a statement on Oct 13, the police said the two Chinese nationals – aged 54 and 59 – were involved in two separate cases of theft on board an aircraft. Officers from the Airport Police Division conducted an operation at Changi Airport Terminal 4 at about 9.45am on Oct 12.

During the operation, the officers arrested the two men after they were found with three bank cards that did not belong to them. Further investigations revealed that the men allegedly stole the bank cards from two passengers during a flight from Ho Chi Minh City to Singapore.
Each man allegedly took the bank cards from a different passenger’s bag in the overhead compartment and disembarked without the victims realising that their cards were missing.

The two men are expected to be charged with theft on board an aircraft. If found guilty, they may be jailed for up to three years, fined, or both. In their statement, the police advised travellers to keep their cash or valuables on them instead of in the overhead compartments.

articles.headline: Australia and Singapore Bolster Cyber Cooperation Amidst AI-Driven Threats
articles.dek: Assistant Minister Matt Thistlethwaite highlights the escalating sophistication of cyberattacks due to AI and emphasizes the critical need for enhanced regional collaboration and protective measures.
articles.lead: Australia's Assistant Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade, Matt Thistlethwaite, has underscored the growing threat posed by artificial intelligence in accelerating cyberattacks and transnational cybercrime. Speaking at the Singapore International Cyber Week, Thistlethwaite noted that AI enables malicious actors to launch sophisticated attacks with unprecedented speed and scale, transforming threats that once took weeks of coding into operations completed in minutes.
articles.takeaway: Assistant Minister Matt Thistlethwaite highlights the escalating sophistication of cyberattacks due to AI and emphasizes the critical need for enhanced regional collaboration and protective measures.
body: Australia's Assistant Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade, Matt Thistlethwaite, has underscored the growing threat posed by artificial intelligence in accelerating cyberattacks and transnational cybercrime. Speaking at the Singapore International Cyber Week, Thistlethwaite noted that AI enables malicious actors to launch sophisticated attacks with unprecedented speed and scale, transforming threats that once took weeks of coding into operations completed in minutes.

Thistlethwaite emphasized that this technological advancement necessitates a parallel increase in governmental capacity to counter these evolving risks. He pointed out that AI is making it easier for cybercriminals to breach critical infrastructure, including power grids, hospitals, and transportation systems, raising significant security concerns. In response, Australia has established an Office of AI to oversee national AI standards and is reinforcing existing laws that mandate cybersecurity measures for critical infrastructure operators.

The minister highlighted the strong cybersecurity partnership between Australia and Singapore, which was recently renewed. This collaboration focuses on enhancing information sharing, conducting joint exercises, and building regional capacity to combat cyber threats. Australia is committed to supporting Singapore as it prepares to chair the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 2027, where cybercrime and AI are expected to be key agenda items.

Furthermore, Australia is investing A$83.5 million over four years to bolster cybersecurity capabilities across the Indo-Pacific region through its Southeast Asia and Pacific Cyber Program. This initiative aims to improve regional preparedness for cyber incidents, enhance training, and develop supportive policies and regulations, with a particular focus on assisting Pacific nations.

Australia is also actively addressing the rise of scam centers in Southeast Asia, which exploit trafficked individuals for online fraud. Initiatives like Operation Firestorm, a collaboration between Australian and Thai authorities, demonstrate a commitment to disrupting these transnational criminal networks. Looking ahead, Australia is working towards ratifying the United Nations Convention against Cybercrime in the first half of 2027, further strengthening international cooperation against cybercrime.

articles.headline: Singapore’s AI-led economic growth set to continue in 2027: MAS

body: Activity in technology-related sectors is expected to moderate next year, but should remain a principal driver of economic growth, said the central bank on Wednesday (Oct 14).

SINGAPORE: Artificial intelligence-driven expansion of Singapore’s economy is projected to continue next year, though the pace of growth may slow down, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said on Wednesday (Oct 14).
Growth should be supported by strong order backlogs and capacity expansions in AI-related production, the central bank said in its latest quarterly macroeconomic review.

While activity may moderate compared with the “exceptional pace” in 2026, it should remain a “principal driver” of growth, said MAS. Singapore’s economy grew 5.4 per cent in the third quarter of the year, after expanding 6.2 per cent in the second quarter, said the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry in its advance estimates on Wednesday.
“The technology-related sectors continued to expand robustly, accounting for around 75 per cent of overall (year-on-year) growth,” MAS said, describing the growth as “relatively concentrated”.

Tech-related sectors experienced “outsized expansion”, while non-tech and non-oil sectors saw “mixed” growth, the report said. The durability of the current economic expansion hinges on three key considerations, said MAS.

SINGAPORE – Working adults looking to upgrade their skills or switch careers will have another avenue for support, with the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) setting up a new school on Sept 1 to help them navigate their working lives.

The SIT School of Lifelong Learning and Career Development, or SITLearn, will help individuals assess existing skills, acquire knowledge and navigate career transitions, while connecting them with potential employers.
It will offer courses developed with industry partners to equip workers with skills in areas such as artificial intelligence and sustainable data centre operations.

Working adults will also be able to tap career guidance to identify skill gaps and plan their next career move. SIT president Chua Kee Chaing said the new school comes as AI reshapes jobs and the skills needed to perform them.

Citing projections by the World Economic Forum, Chua said at SIT’s convocation ceremony on Oct 12 that nearly four in 10 skills used in workplaces today are expected to change or become outdated by 2030.

SINGAPORE – A male primary school teacher has been accused of recording a video of a female individual’s groin area at his workplace. Court documents did not disclose whether she was a pupil or staff member at the school.

The 45-year-old man, who was handed a voyeurism charge on Oct 12, is accused of committing the offence in 2023. Details about the school cannot be disclosed due to a gag order to protect the alleged victim’s identity.

The Straits Times is also not naming the teacher, as doing so could lead to the alleged victim being identified. The man is expected to plead guilty on Nov 30. In response to ST’s queries, the Ministry of Education (MOE) said the man had been suspended from duties since June and is no longer teaching in any school.

An MOE spokesperson said: “(We take) a serious view of staff misconduct and will not hesitate to take disciplinary action against those who fail to adhere to our standards of conduct and discipline, including dismissal from service.” An offender convicted of voyeurism can be jailed for up to two years, fined, caned or receive any combination of such punishments.

In response to queries, the police and the Singapore Civil Defence Force said they were alerted at about 2pm that day to an accident involving a car and a van at Cairnhill Circle, in a slip road leading to the CTE towards the SLE.

articles.headline: New Society Aims to Educate Public on Nuclear Energy
articles.dek: The Nuclear Learning & Understanding Society (NUCLEUS) has been formed to provide factual information and address public concerns about nuclear energy as Singapore considers its adoption.
articles.lead: A new ground-up initiative, the Nuclear Learning & Understanding Society (NUCLEUS), was established in September to foster a better public understanding of nuclear energy. The society aims to share general knowledge about the science and engineering behind nuclear power and explain why governments consider it as an energy source.
articles.takeaway: The Nuclear Learning & Understanding Society (NUCLEUS) has been formed to provide factual information and address public concerns about nuclear energy as Singapore considers its adoption.
body: A new ground-up initiative, the Nuclear Learning & Understanding Society (NUCLEUS), was established in September to foster a better public understanding of nuclear energy. The society aims to share general knowledge about the science and engineering behind nuclear power and explain why governments consider it as an energy source.

NUCLEUS was formed amid ongoing government assessments into the potential adoption of nuclear energy, a topic that can be sensitive and is marked by a gap in public awareness. Matthew Chew, president of NUCLEUS, noted that while many may support the idea of nuclear power in principle, concerns often arise regarding its proximity to residential areas.

Discussions around nuclear waste management are a common point of public interest. Chew clarified that established methods, such as land-based dry casks or deep underground geological storage, are designed to safely contain radioactive waste and prevent exposure to humans and the environment. A 2023 study indicated no major technical obstacles to storing Singapore's potential nuclear waste underground, though further on-site investigations will be necessary.

The society plans to host seminars, workshops, and talks in schools to engage the public on topics including nuclear safety, plant locations, and career opportunities. NUCLEUS emphasizes that its role is not to advocate for or against nuclear energy but to provide a non-judgmental space for learning and asking questions.

NUCLEUS currently comprises 10 members, including individuals with expertise in nuclear science, engineering, and finance. The society aims to bring a layman's perspective to discussions, particularly concerning advanced technologies like small modular reactors (SMRs), which are considered potentially suitable for Singapore's land constraints.

body: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox Workers’ Party MP Jamus Lim was seen sniffling in Parliament last week. SINGAPORE – What began as a noticeable sniffle in Parliament last week has escalated into a hospital stay for Sengkang MP Jamus Lim, who was admitted for “full-blown” pneumonia after catching Influenza A.

In a Facebook post on the morning of Oct 12, the Workers’ Party MP said he had initially intended to take only the remainder of the week off. However, Lim said he had to check into a hospital over the weekend after his blood oxygen level fell to the low 90s.

Blood oxygen saturation, or SpO2, is typically between 95% and 100% in healthy individuals. Lim’s post did not indicate how long he would remain in hospital. Addressing his Anchorvale residents, he referred to a video of himself sniffling away during a parliament sitting on Oct 6.

In the clip, Lim can be seen sniffling while delivering a speech. PAP MP Diana Pang (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights GRC) then comes to his aid with a tissue. In his post, Lim said: “As it turns out, that sniffling eventually developed into a bad case of Influenza A, before culminating in full-blown pneumonia.

“All that to say, while I’m still stuck here, I am unable to attend to my regular MP duties. This includes tonight’s meet-the-people session (MPS), as well as our weekly house visits, estate walks, and coffeeshop chit-chats.

“My capable #TeamSengkang volunteers have kindly agreed to #StepUp, and so MPS will go ahead as usual. In the meantime, I’ll do what I can on the back end to clear all appeal letters and to catch up on my e-mail backlog, but I thank you for your patience in the meantime.” The post was accompanied by a photo of a sign that read: “Temporarily Out of Service.” Daniel Lai is a journalist at the ST Now team, covering breaking news and international affairs.

body: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox SINGAPORE – Thirty people were evacuated and one person was taken to hospital after a fire broke out in a coffee shop in Bukit Batok on the morning of Oct 11.

In response to queries, the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) said it was alerted to the fire at Block 413 Bukit Batok West Avenue 4 at 3.50am. The fire involved three food stalls at a coffee shop on the ground floor, it added.
As a precaution, the police and SCDF evacuated about 30 people from the affected block. SCDF officers entered the coffee shop by force and extinguished the fire using two water jets.

One of the evacuated persons was taken to Ng Teng Fong General Hospital. The cause of the fire is under investigation, said SCDF. In a Facebook post, Hong Kah North MP Lee Hong Chuang said he had visited the affected block, and that he observed “no significant impact” on the residents living on the second floor.

“However, at one unit, I could feel that the floor was slightly warm. I advised the family to exercise extra caution and keep their little one away from the kitchen floor for the time being, as young children’s skin can be more sensitive to heat,” he said.

Lee also said: “Beyond the physical damage within the coffee shop, we must also remember the people whose lives and livelihoods have been affected”. He added that “behind every stall are hardworking individuals and families who need some time to clear up and start over again”.
